title: the mountain ahead
hookLine: the mountain ahead; Nanak's morning prayer
last: THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB — A LIVING BOOK.

lines: THE FIRST THING IN THE DAY.
cards: It's still dark outside. Four in the morning, maybe five. In homes in Punjab, London, Toronto, California and Nairobi, someone is already up.
They've bathed. They sit quietly, cover their head, and begin to recite a long poem, often from memory. Some learned it as children, a verse at a time, beside a grandparent before school.
It's the first thing in the scripture and the first thing in their day.

teach.b: Japji Sahib. Jap, to recite, the same root as naam japna. Ji and Sahib, words of love and respect.
It's Guru Nanak's great poem, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with the root verse from days ten and eleven.

teach.h: THE TRUE ONE WAS IN THE BEGINNING.
teach.b: Then a short verse that the translator Macauliffe gave like this: "The True One was in the beginning; the True One was in the primal age."
Then come thirty-eight stanzas, called pauris, steps or rungs, like a ladder, and a closing verse that pictures air as the Guru, water as the father, and the earth as the great mother of all.
Inside, it's full of questions. Can you think your way to God? Not if you think a hundred thousand times, the first stanza says.
What will do it? Living within hukam, God's will, the word from day seventeen.
It's the first of the daily prayers, and nobody has to start with all of it: many begin with the root verse, then a stanza, then a little more. That's why your line is a promise.
Later on this path, we'll climb Japji verse by verse. And look how far you've come. Waheguru, langar, the turban, the Panj Pyare, Ardas, Sikh, the Khanda.
Seva, Ik Onkar, the root verse, both lines, kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna. Sangat, the gurdwara, chardi kala, the five Ks, Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru Granth Sahib. And now Japji.
Twenty-one words. Camp one is done.

how: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers (Nitnem) recite Japji Sahib each morning, often before dawn after bathing, as the first of them; children often learn it by heart a stanza at a time.

games.q: camp one's words — tap the pairs.
p: a stanza: a step, a rung

s: Japji Sahib begins with the root verse
the Mool Mantar comes first, then a short verse, then thirty-eight stanzas.
the first stanza says you can reach God by thinking hard enough
not if you think a hundred thousand times; the way is living within hukam.
Japji is usually recited in the evening
it's the morning prayer, often said before dawn.

games.q: you want to reach God. the first stanza of Japji weighs your options. which one does it point to?
o: think about it a hundred thousand times.
games.why: thinking won't do it, silence won't, possessions won't. the stanza's answer is walking in the way of hukam.

practice: Sit tall, the way someone sits in the early morning to recite. Picture a mountain path ahead of you, thirty-eight steps rising into the light. You don't have to climb today.
Just stand at the bottom and look up. Then look back down the path you've already walked: twenty-one days, twenty-one words. Breathe with both, what's behind and what's ahead.

wordCard.voice: Japji Sahib. Guru Nanak's morning poem, the first in the scripture: the root verse, thirty-eight stanzas and a closing verse. Twenty-first word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: jap, the title of the poem in the scripture; Japji Sahib adds words of respect.

carryVoice: Your line: 38 stanzas, verse by verse. One rung at a time, starting whenever you like. Tomorrow camp two begins: the stories, starting with a baby born in a small village in 1469.
